comments.body: Interesting usecase, and makes sense to me. /etc/ssh is used by multiple things including both the SSH client and server.

Not sure if we should use `security.pam.services.sudo.sshAgentAuth` or [security.pam.sshAgentAuth.enable](https://search.nixos.org/options?channel=unstable&include_modular_service_options=1&include_nixos_options=1&query=sshagentauth&show=option:security.pam.sshAgentAuth.enable). Also we may want to check that the paths in [security.pam.sshAgentAuth.authorizedKeysFiles](https://search.nixos.org/options?channel=unstable&include_modular_service_options=1&include_nixos_options=1&query=sshagentauth&show=option:security.pam.sshAgentAuth.authorizedKeysFiles) overlap with the authorized_keys.d directories.

I am a fan of something like the second option you proposed, though:

>Alternatively create the /etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/* files only if at least one of security.pam.services.sudo.sshAgentAuth or services.openssh.enable is true.

Notably, it would not be a breaking change.

Any opinions @philiptaron?

issue.body:
### Nixpkgs version

- Stable (25.11)

### Describe the bug

I am using SSH agent auth for passwordless sudo.

My config looks like this:
```
{
  users.users."myuser".openssh.authorizedKeys.keys = [
  "ssh-rsa AAAAB3..... mykey"
  ];

  security.pam.sshAgentAuth.enable = true;
  security.pam.services.sudo.sshAgentAuth = true;
}
```

This works great in combination with `services.openssh.enable = true`,
but on the machines where i don't need a listening openssh daemon and have
```
  environment.systemPackages = with pkgs; [openssh];
  services.openssh.enable = false;
```

 the `/etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/` directory remains empty, which interfers with the operation of ssh agent auth.

A workaround on those hosts is to create the file manually:

```
  # probably because of a bug (?) on this host you manually have to create this file for
  # security.pam.sshAgentAuth to work
  environment.etc."ssh/authorized_keys.d/myuser" = {
    mode = "0444";
    text = "ssh-rsa AAAAB3..... mykey"
  };
```
but now the configuration is redundant and an ugly hack.

Another workaround would be to leave the sshd service enabled but block all incoming connections or block it at the nixos-firewall. But this is also ugly.



### Steps to reproduce

Use the above setting. SSH agent auth based sudo should work. As soon as you disable the SSHD service, which should be independent of the ssh client, the auth stops working.

### Expected behaviour

The file `/etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/myuser` should be created as long as `users.users."myuser".openssh.authorizedKeys.keys` is set, regardless of the setting of `services.openssh.enable`.

Alternatively create the `/etc/ssh/authorized_keys.d/*` files only if at least one of `security.pam.services.sudo.sshAgentAuth` or `services.openssh.enable` is `true`.
